'''Joanna Aizenberg''' (born 1960) is a professor of [[chemistry]] and [[chemical biology]] at [[Harvard University]]. She is the Amy Smith Berylson Professor of [[Materials Science]] at Harvard's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.iinano.org/Joanna-Aizenberg|title=Joanna Aizenberg {{!}} International Institute for Nanotechnology|website=www.iinano.org|access-date=2017-09-14|archive-date=2015-01-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150108143326/http://www.iinano.org/Joanna-Aizenberg|url-status=dead}}</ref> the co-director of the [[Kavli Institute|Kavli Institute for Bionano Science and Technology]] and a core faculty member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]].<ref name="harvard1">{{cite web|url=http://chemistry.harvard.edu/people/joanna-aizenberg |title=Joanna Aizenberg &#124; Department of Chemistry & Chemical Biology |publisher=Chemistry.harvard.edu |date= |accessdate=2014-08-20}}</ref> She is a prominent figure in the field of biologically inspired materials science, having authored ~240 publications and holding ~70 patents.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wyss.harvard.edu/viewpage/118/joanna-aizenberg |title=Joanna Aizenberg : Wyss Institute at Harvard |publisher=Wyss.harvard.edu |accessdate=2014-08-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090808121451/http://wyss.harvard.edu/viewpage/118/joanna-aizenberg |archive-date=2009-08-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-08-05 |title=Joanna Aizenberg, Ph.D. |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/associate-faculty/joanna-aizenberg/ |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Education==
[[File:Joanna Aizenberg materials.webm|left|thumb|Joanna Aizenberg discusses creating every desired material]]
Aizenberg received her B.S. degree in chemistry and her [[M.S.]] degree in [[physical chemistry]] from [[Moscow State University]] in 1981 and 1984 respectively, and her [[Ph.D]]. degree in [[structural biology]] from the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] in 1996.<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
She did her postdoctoral research with [[George M. Whitesides|George Whitesides]] at Harvard University, investigating micro/nanofabrication and [[near-field optics]]. In 1998, she joined [[Bell Labs]] as a member of the technical staff where she has made a number of pioneering contributions, including developing new biomimetic approaches for the synthesis of ordered mineral films with highly controlled shapes and orientations, and discovering unique biological optical systems that outperform technological analogs, as well as characterizing the associated organic molecules.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/private/person.asp?personId=275927299&privcapId=275614973&previousCapId=4016263&previousTitle=ENMAX%20Corp.|title=Joanna Aizenberg Ph.D.: Executive Profile & Biography - Bloomberg|website=www.bloomberg.com|access-date=2017-09-14}}</ref>

In 2007, Aizenberg joined the [[Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences]].<ref name="harvard1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Harvard Portrait – Joanna Aizenberg|url=http://harvardmagazine.com/2008/07/joanna-aizenberg.html|accessdate=20 August 2014|work=Harvard Magazine|issue=July–August 2008|publisher=Harvard Magazine Inc.|date=2008}}</ref>

The lab's research investigates a wide range of topics that include biomimetics, self-assembly, adaptive materials, crystal engineering, surface wettability, nanofabrication, biooptics, biomaterials, and biomechanics.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aizenberglab.seas.harvard.edu/index.php?show=research |title=The Aizenberg Biomineralization and Biomimetics Lab |publisher=Aizenberglab.seas.harvard.edu |date= |accessdate=2014-08-20}}</ref>

In 2019, Aizenberg was elected into the [[National Academy of Engineering]] for contributions to the understanding of biological systems and bioinspired materials design.
